meaning: Truth, rightness, correctness, measure. Root of Maat (mꜣꜥt), the cosmic principle of truth and order

phonemes.desc: Bilabial nasal [m], the first consonant of the root for truth, straightness, and measure
Egyptological alef, a glottal stop or voiced pharyngeal placeholder; the exact value is debated, but it closes the root mꜣ
Long open vowel [aː], supplied by convention; the hieroglyphs record only m-ꜣ

pronunciation.approximation: MAH-ʿA — a prolonged 'ma' followed by a slight catch in the throat where the alef sits.

pronunciation.note: Mꜣ is the monosyllabic root from which the goddess Mꜣꜥt ('Maat') is derived. The Unicode form preserves the Egyptological alef (ꜣ) as the registrable stand-in for the final consonant. It is Tier 1: the Egyptological alef (ꜣ) is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: The Straight Line
domains.subtitle: Truth, Measure, and Cosmic Order
domains.lead: Mꜣ is the Egyptian root for what is straight, true, right, and in measure. It is not merely an abstract virtue; it is the line against which the cosmos, society, and the individual life are tested. From this root comes Mꜣꜥt, the goddess of truth, whose feather is weighed against the heart of the dead. To say mꜣ is to invoke the standard by which all things are judged.

cards.name: The Feather of Truth
cards.desc: The ostrich feather of Mꜣꜥt is weighed against the deceased's heart in the judgment hall of Osiris.

cards.name: Straightness and Measure
cards.desc: Mꜣ governs geometry, law, and the moral axis that keeps maat from slipping into isfet (chaos).

cards.name: Cosmic Order
cards.desc: Kings rule by upholding mꜣꜥt; the sun's daily course, the Nile's flood, and justice on earth all depend on it.

cards.name: Judicial Testimony
cards.desc: In temple oaths and legal documents, one swears by mꜣꜥt; to lie is to throw the cosmos out of alignment.

mythology.lead: Mꜣ has no independent mythic biography because it is the principle that makes biography possible. It appears in every major Egyptian funerary and royal text as the standard against which lives, deeds, and even gods are measured. Its personification, Mꜣꜥt, sits in the solar barque and stands at the throne of every legitimate king.

myths.title: The Weighing of the Heart
myths.text: Spell 125 of the Book of the Dead stages the most famous judgment scene of the ancient world. The deceased enters the Hall of the Two Truths, faces Osiris enthroned among the forty-two assessor gods, and delivers the Negative Confession — the great litany in which he denies, one by one, theft, murder, falsehood, adultery, and every act that disturbs mꜣꜥt. Then the moment of test: Anubis sets his heart on the scales against the single ostrich feather of Mꜣꜥt, while Thoth stands ready to record the result. If the heart is light, the justified dead pass into the beautiful west; if heavy with wrongdoing, the composite monster Ammit — crocodile head, lion torso, hippopotamus hindquarters — waits beside the scales to devour it, and the soul is annihilated, denied even the afterlife it petitioned for. The most celebrated witness is the Papyrus of Ani (c. 1250 BCE, British Museum), whose vignette has taught the scene to every generation since Champollion. The myth's claim is stark: at the end, nothing you owned is weighed — only what you did, against a feather.

myths.title: Mꜣꜥt in the Barque of Ra
myths.text: Egyptian temple theology never lets the sun simply shine. Hymns and ritual scenes from the New Kingdom onward place Mꜣꜥt beside Ra in the solar barque: the creator sails the sky in a boat whose steersman is Truth herself, and Spell 17 of the Book of the Dead identifies the eye of Ra with mꜣꜥt. When the barque descends into the Duat each night, the serpent Apophis — isfet, chaos, the lie given serpent form — attacks it at every hour, and the order of the cosmos survives only because the god and his company hold to the standard. Kings performed the daily rite of presenting a small figure of Mꜣꜥt to the temple god, a gesture the inscriptions gloss plainly: 'I offer you Maat; I satisfy her for you' — the monarch paying truth as tribute, renewing the cosmic contract each dawn. The myth encodes a physics: light is not the default state of things but an achievement, re-won every night against the forces of disorder.

myths.title: The King as Upholder of Mꜣꜥt
myths.text: Every pharaoh ruled as the earthly guardian of mꜣꜥt, and Egyptian wisdom literature turns the doctrine into instruction. The Instruction for Merikare, a Middle Kingdom king's testament addressed to his son, commands: nourish your people as a shepherd tends his flock, for 'a ruler who rules by mꜣꜥt' is the one whose memorial endures; the speaker warns against unjust seizure, because a single act of violence breeds a generation of disorder. Temple reliefs make the same argument in stone: the king, tiny before the god, presents the figure of Mꜣꜥt — the world kept in balance, offered back to its source. Coronation rites, the Sed jubilee, and the daily cult all rehearsed this offering, so that kingship itself became a liturgy of maintenance. The doctrine even had a fiscal face, for taxes, boundaries, and Nile gauges were all instruments of the same straightness. The myth's political meaning is exact: legitimacy is not inherited but performed, every day, as the visible upkeep of order.

myths.title: The Eloquent Peasant Pleads for Maat
myths.text: The Middle Kingdom Tale of the Eloquent Peasant — preserved in four papyri including Papyrus Berlin 3023 and Papyrus Butler — is the great narrative of mꜣꜥt from below. A poor peasant named Khunanup, travelling to market, is robbed by the steward Nemtynakht, who seizes his donkeys and goods by a legal trick; the peasant petitions the high steward Rensi, and his nine petitions are masterpieces of rhetoric in which he argues not for charity but for rectification. Do mꜣꜥt for the lord of mꜣꜥt, he pleads; the balance is the lord's own scale — rob not the poor man of his goods, for a man's goods are the breath of his nostrils. The tale delays its justice deliberately: King Nebkaure orders the petitions kept for the record, so that the peasant must speak until the ideal is fully articulated. When judgment finally comes, the peasant is compensated and the steward's goods given to him — yet the tale's fame rests on the speaking, not the verdict. The myth defines mꜣꜥt from the victim's side: order is not what the powerful declare but what the wronged can make them hear.

lore.syncretism: Mꜣ is almost always expanded into the goddess Mꜣꜥt in cult and art, yet the root itself underlies Egyptian ethics, law, and cosmology in a way no single deity-name can hold. Greeks and Romans, meeting the weighing of the heart, identified Mꜣꜥt with Dikē, their personified Justice, and through that identification the feathered scale passed into the iconography of later Mediterranean judgment — the psychostasia leaves its trace in Christian and Islamic images of the weighing of souls. In the Hellenistic period, Egyptian priests composed aretalogies of Isis that fold maat's functions into a Greek frame, while Hermetic literature re-reads the straight line as a metaphysical principle. Modern discussions of Egyptian philosophy cite mꜣꜥt as among the earliest systematic concepts of cosmic justice anywhere, and the Afrocentric renewal associated with Maulana Karenga's 'Nguzo Saba' deliberately names its first principle Umoja-imbued 'Maat' for truth, balance, and reciprocity. The root's career is unusual: it was never translated away, only absorbed.
lore.culturalLegacy: The root mꜣ survives in every museum exhibit of the Book of the Dead — the judgment vignette is among the most reproduced images of the ancient world — and in every account of Egyptian ethics, from Assmann's study of Gerechtigkeit und Unsterblichkeit to the museum label beside the Papyrus of Ani. Its personification, Maat, has become an international emblem of justice, balance, and ecological harmony; her feather appears on the logos of law firms, human-rights groups, and environmental movements. Contemporary Kemetic and pan-African circles speak of 'living in maat', consciously drawing on the ancient idea that truth is not verbal honesty alone but the active maintenance of order against entropy, greed, and deceit. In Egyptology itself the word remains a working term of art — 'acting according to maat' is still how scholars gloss legitimate rule. Few monosyllables have carried so long a shadow.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Mꜣ is the Egyptian word for the straight line in a crooked world. It asks not only that we tell the truth but that we measure our lives against a standard larger than desire or power. The hieroglyph itself is an image of measuring — the builder's plummet, the level — a tool dragged into metaphysics and made to weigh hearts.

In the Hall of Judgment it is not wealth or fame that is weighed; it is the lightness of a heart that did not lie, steal, or break the social bond. That image remains the most demanding vision of accountability ever drawn: a single feather as the counterweight of a whole life. To restore mꜣ in Unicode is to restore a word that still judges us — and that asks, every dawn, whether the world we are making is straight.

lore.archaeology: The concept of mꜣꜥt is ubiquitous in Pharaonic material culture: ostrich-feather amulets in funerary assemblages, tomb paintings of the psychostasia, royal offering scenes in temples from Karnak to Edfu, and papyri of the Book of the Dead. The Papyrus of Ani and the Book of the Dead of Hunefer (British Museum) are the most famous visual witnesses. Temples of Maat existed within larger complexes — most famously the small temple of Maat at Karnak — and judges, viziers, and treasurers bore titles invoking mꜣꜥt, while balance-pan weights inscribed with her feather turn the metaphor into metrology. The root's material footprint is, fittingly, exactly the footprint of a standard.
